subject: Chemistry
title: Karen Wetterhahn: A Drop of Dimethylmercury
description: A quick, practical guide to Karen Wetterhahn: A Drop of Dimethylmercury.

hook.text: In 1996, a single drop of dimethylmercury fell on Karen Wetterhahn's glove. She died ten months later.

buildup.text: Wetterhahn was a chemistry professor at Dartmouth studying toxic metals. She wore standard latex gloves and a lab coat.

discovery.text: Dimethylmercury passes through latex gloves in seconds. It penetrates skin instantly and attacks the nervous system.

twist.text: Symptoms appeared five months later: slurred speech, loss of balance, blindness. By then, mercury had destroyed her brain.

climax.text: Her death changed lab safety worldwide. Thicker laminate gloves and fume hoods are now required for organomercury compounds.

punchline.text: One drop through a glove. The most toxic organic mercury compound killed an expert.

quiz.question: Why was dimethylmercury so dangerous despite Wetterhahn wearing gloves?
options: It passes through standard latex gloves in seconds and absorbs through skin instantly
The glove had an invisible tear that she didn't notice
She accidentally inhaled vapors when she removed the glove

details.summary: In 1996 Dartmouth professor Karen Wetterhahn accidentally spilled a few drops of dimethylmercury on her latex gloves during a routine experiment. The chemical penetrated the gloves in seconds, was absorbed through her skin, and caused fatal mercury poisoning that killed her ten months later.
details.whyItMatters: Wetterhahn's death revealed that standard latex gloves provided no protection against dimethylmercury and changed laboratory safety protocols for handling highly toxic organometallic compounds worldwide.
takeaways: Dimethylmercury penetrates latex gloves in under 15 seconds
A few drops absorbed through skin delivered a lethal mercury dose
Her death led to mandatory laminate gloves for organomercury work

faq.question: Why is dimethylmercury so much more dangerous than regular mercury?
faq.answer: Dimethylmercury is an organic mercury compound that easily penetrates biological barriers including skin, gloves, and the blood-brain barrier. Once absorbed, it converts to methylmercury and accumulates in the brain. Its lipophilicity allows it to bypass protections that block elemental mercury.

faq.question: What safety changes resulted from Wetterhahn's death?
faq.answer: OSHA and universities worldwide banned the use of latex and nitrile gloves for dimethylmercury work, requiring laminate or Silver Shield gloves instead. Many institutions eliminated dimethylmercury from their procedures entirely, substituting less toxic mercury reference standards.
